sections.h2: Where is Franklin, Tennessee, and how fast has it grown?
sections.html:
Williamson County's government sits in Franklin, about 21 miles south of Nashville along the Harpeth River, and only six Tennessee cities have more people. The Census Bureau lists 62,487 people in 2010, 83,454 in 2020 and 90,226 in its July 2025 estimate, an increase of 8.0 percent over the 2020 base. The city covers 42.75 square miles of land, which works out to roughly 1,952 residents per square mile at the 2020 count.

Franklin's population is more than five times what it was in 1980, when 12,407 people lived here. That rise came as northern Franklin filled with houses and offices, and as the city became a Nashville suburb with its own jobs. Anyone thinking about selling a Franklin house is working in a city that has changed fast within a single generation.

sections.h2: What in Franklin's history still shows up in its houses?
sections.html:
Abram Maury Jr. founded the town on October 26, 1799, and named it for Benjamin Franklin. The Second Battle of Franklin on November 30, 1864 produced nearly 10,000 casualties and turned forty-four buildings into temporary field hospitals. The Carter, Carnton and Lotz houses from that era still stand.

Five of the city's historic districts carry National Register listings, and older buildings and neighborhoods get protection under local ordinance. A former stove factory, the Dortch Stove Works of 1928 that later made Magic Chef ranges, was restored in the late 1990s and now holds offices, restaurants and retail space.

An owner near the square or inside a historic district should ask City Hall which rules apply before planning exterior repairs.

sections.h2: Which employers and roads support Franklin's housing market?
sections.html:
Franklin has a deep base of health care and corporate employers. The city's 2024 annual financial report ranks its ten biggest employers, and the top five are below.

Interstate 65 crosses the eastern side of the city with four exits, and US 31 and US 431 run together toward Nashville. State Routes 96, 246 and 441 fan out from Franklin, and the Mack Hatcher Parkway bypass circles the business district to the east. Cool Springs Boulevard and McEwen Drive both have interchanges with I-65.

The city's 2026-27 budget message says a 10-year capital plan of $458 million is 82 percent devoted to transportation, including a state partnership to widen Mack Hatcher Parkway Southeast, the widening of McEwen Road and a new City Hall on the downtown square.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers say about Franklin homes?
sections.html:
QuickFacts puts the typical Franklin owner-occupied house at $705,400 for the 2020 to 2024 period, more than double the $332,700 national median. Owners with a mortgage report monthly costs of $2,542, and owners without one report $712. Renters pay a median of $1,923. Of the city's 33,998 households, 63.8 percent own their home.

Household income has a median of $119,528, and 64.5 percent of residents past age 25 have finished at least a bachelor's degree. About 84.6 percent of people were at the same address a year before the survey. Those figures describe a market with long-staying owners and large price tags.

sections.h2: What does a Franklin homeowner pay in property tax?
sections.html:
The city charges $0.296 for each $100 of assessed value, and the proposed 2026-27 budget leaves that unchanged. The rate has two parts: a $0.2310 base for operations and debt, plus $0.0650 added after the last reappraisal for infrastructure and city services. The city calls its rate one of the lowest in Tennessee. The county assessor reappraises every four years.

The Williamson County Trustee bills for the county, the Franklin Special School District and the city together. Here is how the county's published schedule works:

  • Statements are mailed in early October.
  • Payment opens the first Monday of October and stays open through the end of February.
  • From March 1, a 1.5 percent interest charge starts, then repeats on the first of every later month.
  • The trustee cannot waive, prorate or release any tax or interest.
  • Whoever owned the property on January 1 is the owner of record who gets the bill, so a seller closing mid-year must pass it on to the buyer.

As an example, a Franklin house assessed at 25 percent of a $700,000 value carries $175,000 of assessed value, and the city's share comes to $518. County and school charges are on top of that, so ask the trustee at 615-790-5709 for the full figure on a specific parcel.

sections.h2: Which schools and colleges serve Franklin?
sections.html:
Most of the city belongs to the Franklin Special School District for kindergarten through eighth grade, and high school students attend Williamson County Schools. Outlying parts of the city are in the county district for every grade.

  • Private schools include Battle Ground Academy, Franklin Classical School, Franklin Christian Academy, Montessori School of Franklin, New Hope Academy and Thales Academy.
  • Higher education includes the Columbia State Community College campus that opened in 2016, a Belmont University campus at the Williamson Center, a Lipscomb University SPARK site, New College Franklin and Williamson College.

Families often start a house search with the school boundary, so a seller should be ready to tell a buyer which district serves the address.

sections.h2: What city fees and utilities will a Franklin buyer ask about?
sections.html:
Buyers often ask about monthly costs, and Franklin's budget documents answer part of the question. Residential trash and recycling is set to rise by $1 to $34 a month in fiscal 2027, and stormwater fees are projected to add about $20.70 a year for most homes. Water and sewer rates rose 6 percent and 5.7 percent on January 1, 2026.

The city's water department serves most residents, though pockets are served by the Mallory Valley, Milcrofton and HB&TS utility districts. Electricity comes from Middle Tennessee Electric through TVA power, and gas from Atmos Energy. A seller should know which provider serves the address before a buyer asks.

sections.h2: Where is a Franklin deed recorded, and what does recording cost?
sections.html:
Deeds for Franklin houses are filed with the Williamson County Register of Deeds at 1320 West Main Street, Suite 201, Franklin, with weekday hours of 8 to 4:30. The office posts a fee calculator and an electronic filing option and answers at 615-790-5706. The county assessor, at 615-790-5708, handles questions about assessed value and the mailing address on a bill.

Recording also triggers state tax. Revenue Department rates apply to the paperwork: 37 cents for every $100 of the sale price as realty transfer tax, and 11.5 cents per $100 of a buyer's loan above the first $2,000 as mortgage tax. The register collects both and sends them on to the state.

Anyone selling a Franklin house for cash, through an agent or on their own should have the title company confirm the payoff, the unpaid taxes and the recording steps before closing day.

faqs.a: About 90,226 people lived there as of July 2025, based on the Census Bureau estimate, after a 2020 count of 83,454. Only a handful of Tennessee cities are bigger.

faqs.q: What is Franklin's city property tax rate?
faqs.a: It is $0.296 per $100, and the proposed 2026-27 budget keeps it there. County and school district charges appear on the same bill.

faqs.q: When are Williamson County property taxes due?
faqs.a: They can be paid from the first Monday of October until the end of February. After that, interest of 1.5 percent is added and repeats monthly.

faqs.q: Who pays Tennessee's transfer tax on a Franklin sale?
faqs.a: The buyer does, as the grantee on the deed. The state rate is 37 cents per $100 of price, collected by the register at filing.

faqs.q: Which office records a deed for a Franklin house?
faqs.a: The Williamson County Register of Deeds, in Suite 201 at 1320 West Main Street. Staff there can answer fee questions at 615-790-5706.
